extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary biography / Romantic-era literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a biographical supplement containing S. T. Coleridge's letters and the author's commentary; includes remarks about composition, publication strategy, and poetic qualities. The page is narrative/epistolary rather than an explicit how-to, but it embeds several craft- and publication-related maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good writing principle: language before forced invention
rubrics_metrics.description: "Good writing is produced more effectually by rapidly glancing the language as it already exists, than by a hasty recourse to the mint of invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge asserts a compositional principle: effective prose/poetry often emerges from an intuitive engagement with the existing idiom and available language rather than from deliberate, forced invention. This functions as advice about craft and process (favor idiomatic fluency and rapid composition over contrived novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience alignment: tailor form and content to subscribers/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: "You wish to have one long essay — so should I wish; but so do not my subscribers wish." and "In London and Bristol The Watchman is read for its original matter... The people of Liverpool, Manchester, and Birmingham, &c., take it as a newspaper, and regard the essays and poems as intruders unwished for and unwelcome."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge emphasizes adapting publication format and content to audience expectations and regional reading habits. A writer/editor should consider what subscribers want (e.g., shorter pieces vs. long essays, original commentary vs. news) to maximize reception and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motto for miscellanies: 'ut pia cuique' (to each his own)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In so miscellaneous a collection as I have presented to the Public, ut pia cuique should be the motto."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling a mixed collection, provide a variety of kinds of pieces to meet diverse tastes rather than trying to impose uniformity; editorial pluralism helps address varied reader preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic quality criteria: versification, sublimity, and epic dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Religious Musings has more mind than the Introduction of B. H. of Joan of Arc ... but its versification is not equally rich. It has more passages of sublimity, but it has not that air of severe dignity which characterizes my epic slice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge differentiates poetic virtues: intellectual/depth ('mind'), the technical richness of versification, moments of sublimity, and an overarching 'severe dignity' appropriate to epic tone. Use these dimensions to evaluate or aim for different poetic aims (lyric sublimity vs. epic dignity vs. versification richness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended readership and difficulty: write for your target reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poem was not written for common readers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the intended audience and the appropriate level of metaphysical or technical density. Some works may intentionally eschew broad accessibility in favor of profundity aimed at a more learned readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication strategy: original matter attracts metropolitan readers
rubrics_metrics.description: "In London and Bristol The Watchman is read for its original matter — the news and debate barely tolerated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original, distinctive content is what attracts certain urban/metropolitan readerships; if aiming for impact in such markets, prioritize novel argumentation or exclusive material over filler news that some audiences will ignore.
